title: How do you prepare training records for an FDA inspection?
seoTitle: Training records for an FDA inspection
description: What FDA investigators look at for training under the Investigations Operations Manual and 21 CFR 211.25, with a document checklist for drug and device sites.
shortAnswer: To prepare training records for a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) inspection, map each role to the 21 CFR 211.25 training it requires, prove supervisors' qualifications, link each completion to the procedure version in force, retrieve electronic training data through validated queries, and be ready to explain your new hire and refresher programs. FDA investigators focus on training when an observed deficiency suggests people were not adequately trained, so records must connect training to the work.
keyTakeaways: The FDA Investigations Operations Manual (IOM) tells investigators that a firm's training programs are of particular significance when findings suggest people were not adequately trained.
Under drug Compliance Program 7356.002, training and qualification are evaluated inside each of the six inspected systems, not as a standalone topic.

21 CFR 211.25 requires training in particular operations and in current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), conducted by qualified individuals, continuously and often enough that employees stay familiar with the requirements.
Electronic training records must be produced without delay; investigators are told to assume a firm's custom query logic is unvalidated and to check that no data has been omitted.
A written response to a Form FDA 483 within 15 business days may affect FDA's decision on further action, so plan training remediation evidence in advance.

sections.heading: What do FDA investigators look at for training?

blocks.text: FDA investigators look at training mainly to explain deficiencies they have already observed: whether the people involved were trained on the procedure, whether their supervisors were qualified, and whether the firm's new hire and refresher programs could have prevented the problem. The [2026 Investigations Operations Manual](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/inspection-references/investigations-operations-manual), which FDA describes as the primary operational reference for its investigators, sets this out in Chapter 5.

blocks.title: IOM 5.7.1.4.7, Firm's Training Program
blocks.text: "A firm's training programs are of particular significance when making inspectional findings revealing that people may not be adequately trained." Investigators are told to explain the firm's training program as it correlates to observed deficiencies, to consider an overview of new hire and ongoing refresher training, and to report any specific regulatory training requirements the firm is subject to and how it meets them.

Section 5.6.3.3 of the IOM adds a second line of inquiry: investigators obtain the educational and experience backgrounds of people in key managerial, production, control, and sanitation positions, and ascertain the experience and training of supervisory personnel in terms that describe their qualifications. That is the evidence FDA uses to establish who had the duty and power to prevent or correct a violation.

For drug manufacturers, [Compliance Program 7356.002](https://www.fda.gov/media/75167/download) (implementation date October 17, 2022) states that organization and personnel, "including appropriate qualifications and training," are evaluated as part of each system's operation. Its quality system coverage lists training and qualification of employees in CGMP, including quality functions, risk management, and the specific CGMP operations assigned to individual employees. Training and qualification of personnel also appear in the materials, production, packaging and labeling, and laboratory system checklists.

sections.heading: Which regulations set the training standard the investigator applies?

blocks.text: For finished pharmaceuticals the standard is [21 CFR 211.25](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211/subpart-B): personnel need education, training, and experience to perform their functions; training covers the particular operations they perform and CGMP, including the regulations and written procedures; it is conducted by qualified individuals on a continuing basis and with sufficient frequency; supervisors must be qualified; and there must be an adequate number of qualified personnel. The full requirement is explained on the [FDA GMP personnel training page](/regulations/fda-gmp-personnel-training-requirements).

items: **Records availability:** 21 CFR 211.180(c) requires records to be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period.

**Electronic systems:** 21 CFR 11.10(i) requires a determination that people who develop, maintain, or use electronic record and signature systems have the education, training, and experience for their tasks. See the [Part 11 training page](/regulations/21-cfr-part-11-training-requirements).

**Clinical investigations:** FDA's October 2024 question and answer guidance on electronic systems says FDA may review records of staff training on electronic systems during clinical investigator inspections.

**Medical devices:** since February 2, 2026 the [Quality Management System Regulation](/regulations/fda-qmsr-training-requirements) incorporates ISO 13485:2016, whose clause 6.2 requires competence based on education, training, skills, and experience.

sections.heading: How will the investigator ask for training records?

blocks.text: Expect requests during the inspection for specific people's training files, and possibly a records request before the inspection. The IOM notes that section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act provides for records or other information to be requested in advance of a drug inspection.

items: **Targeted pulls.** The investigator names an operator, analyst, or supervisor linked to an observation and asks for their training history on the relevant procedure.

**System queries.** For electronic learning or quality systems, IOM 5.6.6.1 tells investigators to have firm personnel run queries specific to the information of interest, provide the parameters used, and transmit the data securely. Investigators are told to assume query logic is not validated and to make sure no data has been omitted.
**Supervisor qualification.** Curricula vitae, job descriptions, and qualification records for supervisors of the areas inspected.

**Timeliness.** Under IOM 5.5.2.3, if a drug or device firm delays producing records without a reasonable explanation (such as time to compile a large volume or translate records), the investigator may cite section 501(j) of the Act, which concerns adulteration.

sections.heading: What documents should be ready before the inspection?

blocks.text: Prepare a training evidence set that lets anyone trace a named person from role to procedure version to completion to qualification, within minutes. The table below is an original checklist built from the IOM, CP 7356.002, and 21 CFR 211.25.

sections.heading: What is the step by step preparation method?

blocks.text: Work backward from the areas FDA is most likely to inspect and the deviations already in your system, because those are where training questions start.

items: List open and recent deviations, complaints, and corrective and preventive actions (CAPAs) whose root cause cites training. Confirm each retraining is complete and documented, as covered in [using training in a CAPA](/guides/how-to-use-training-in-a-capa).
For each system in CP 7356.002 likely to be covered, sample five people and trace them from role to procedure to completed training on the version in force on the dates they performed the work.

Check that procedure revisions triggered retraining before the effective date. Gaps here are easier to find with [version control for training content](/guides/how-to-maintain-version-control-for-training-content).
Collect supervisor and trainer qualification files for every area in scope.
Write and test the learning system queries you will run for an investigator, and record their parameters.
Brief subject matter experts so they can describe the new hire and refresher program accurately, since IOM 5.7.1.4.7 asks investigators to report it.
Record any gap you find, remediate it, and keep the original record unchanged. Never backdate training.

sections.heading: What happens to training findings after the inspection?

blocks.text: Significant training deficiencies are written on a Form FDA 483, Inspectional Observations, at the close of the inspection. The IOM instructs investigators to discuss observations with management as they are observed or daily, and to note repeat observations from a prior inspection. Under CP 7356.002, an observation common to several systems, such as personnel qualifications and training, is listed under the first system reported.

The IOM tells investigators to advise management that an adequate response received within 15 business days of the end of the inspection may affect FDA's determination of the need for further action. A credible response to a training observation shows the root cause, retraining with effectiveness checks, the procedure or matrix change that prevents recurrence, and a review of whether the gap affected other people or products. The general method for building these packs is in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each procedure version to the roles that use it, the training built from it, and the assessment evidence for each person, so a single trace answers the investigator's question about who was trained on what version and when. See [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence) and [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Does FDA require a specific format for training records?
faqs.a: No format is prescribed in 21 CFR 211.25. What matters is that records show training in the particular operations and CGMP, by qualified individuals, often enough, and that they are readily available for inspection under 211.180(c). Electronic records must meet Part 11 where they are used to satisfy a records requirement.

faqs.q: Can an FDA investigator log into our learning management system?
faqs.a: Generally no. IOM 5.6.6.1 tells investigators not to personally access a firm's system except in defined bioresearch monitoring and biologics situations. Instead, they oversee firm staff accessing the system, ask for specific queries, and request the query parameters and a secure copy of the data.

faqs.q: Is attendance at a training session enough evidence?
faqs.a: Attendance shows exposure, not that a person can do the job. FDA's 2006 Quality Systems guidance expects training programs to include evaluation of effectiveness, and investigators who see an operator deviate from a procedure will ask how the firm knew that person was competent.

faqs.q: Who should speak to the investigator about the training program?
faqs.a: The person accountable for the training system, usually in quality, should describe the program, with area supervisors available to explain how training works on the floor. Answers should match the written procedure, because the investigator compares the description with the records sampled.

factCheck.claim: IOM is the primary operational reference for FDA investigators; 2026 IOM; content current as of 07/15/2026.

IOM 5.7.1.4.7 verbatim: a firm's training programs are of particular significance when findings reveal people may not be adequately trained; explain program as it correlates to deficiencies; overview of new-hire and ongoing refresher training; report specific regulatory training requirements.
IOM 5.6.3.3: obtain educational and experience backgrounds of key managerial, production, control and sanitation personnel; ascertain experience and training of supervisory personnel.

IOM 5.6.6.1: do not personally access firm systems except BIMO/biologics criteria; oversee firm personnel, request specific queries, parameters, secure transmission; assume query logic is not validated and ensure no data omitted.
IOM 5.5.2.3: for drug or device inspections, delays in producing records without reasonable explanation (compiling large volume, translation) may prompt reference to section 501(j).
IOM 5.10.2.1: section 704(a)(4) provides for a records request in advance of an inspection.

IOM 5.5.10.1: discuss observations as observed or daily; note uncorrected prior or recurring observations on the FDA 483. IOM closing meeting text: advise management that an adequate response within 15 business days of end of inspection may impact FDA's determination of need for subsequent action.

CP 7356.002 (implementation 10/17/2022): organization and personnel including qualifications and training evaluated within each system; quality system includes training/qualification of employees in CGMP covering quality functions, risk management and specific CGMP operations; training/qualification listed in materials, production, packaging/labeling and laboratory systems; observations common to multiple systems (training) listed under first system reported.
211.25(a)-(c), 211.34 consultant records, 211.180(c) records readily available (reused from FDA GMP personnel page factCheck).
